Architecture Princip
les
  
These architectural principles provide a structured framework to guide the modernisation of the legacy BSE application into a resilient, secure, and cloud
 
native platform. They ensure that the solution remains user
 
centred, value
 
driven, and aligned with Defra’s strategic technology direction. Each principle supports a key aspect of effective architecture
 
delivery discipline, user experience, operational efficiency, data clarity, collaboration, security, innovation, and the adoption of fit
 
for
 
purpose technologies. Together, they establish a strong foundation for 
consist decision
-
making, sustainable design, and long
 
term service evolution as the application transitions into a modern cloud environment.
1. Delivery
‑
Focused Architecture
The architecture is designed with a clear and time
‑
bound mandate: to migrate the legacy Windows Server 2016 and IIS
‑
based application to a modern, cloud
‑
native platform by Q3
-
Q4 2026. This provides a defined delivery horizon and ensures alignment with overarching modernisation programmes. The solution embraces iterative discovery, where continuous engagement with business subject matter experts, legacy application (LAP) teams, and delivery partners enables validation of assumptions, identification of unknowns, and refinement of requirements over time. Governance is embedded throughout, with the architecture progressing through Defra’s established SDA, TDA, and CTWG review processes, ensuring that all decisions are transparent, validated, and aligned with enterprise standards.
2. Design for Users
The design places the end users at the centre of the modernisation strategy. A detailed analysis of current BSE application usage and workflows ensures that essential business processes are preserved while opportunities for simplification and efficiency are introduced. Recognising existing operational constraints, the architecture introduces dedicated non
‑
production environments that support functional testing, regression validation, and change assurance. This addresses the long-standing limitation where testing has been conducted in production, significantly reducing risk and improving confidence in releases.
3. Maximise Value, Minimise Waste
A core objective of the architecture is to reduce long
‑
standing technical debt and operational overhead. Migrating away from Windows Server 2016, IIS 10, and manually configured components eliminates unsupported platforms, high maintenance effort, and duplication across environments. Fragmented IIS application pools, custom scripts, and inconsistent deployment patterns are rationalised into a unified, maintainable cloud architecture. By adopting cloud
‑
native services aligned with the Cloud Centre of Excellence (CCoE), the solution enhances scalability, resilience, and cost efficiency, ensuring that investment focuses on value rather than sustaining obsolete technologies.
4. Clean Data, Clear Decisions
The architecture promotes informed decision
‑
making through clarity, accuracy, and transparency of data. Findings from discovery—including application configurations, integrations, interface mappings, and operational dependencies—are consolidated into a single repository, establishing a definitive source of truth. This centralised view enables effective classification of components as active, redundant, or in need of remediation, significantly reducing ambiguity and migration risk. To safeguard the integrity of business processes, the transition includes structured regression testing and validation of data flows, ensuring that outputs remain accurate, reliable, and aligned with business expectations after migration.
5. Connect and Collaborate
The architecture acknowledges the complexity of the existing landscape, which spans multiple stakeholders, legacy systems, and operational dependencies. It is intentionally designed to integrate within this environment while promoting collaboration across delivery teams. Architectural decisions and artefacts are progressed through Defra’s governance forums—SDA, TDA, and CTWG—ensuring shared ownership, transparent decision-making, and alignment across organisations. Additionally, historically scattered documentation, including IIS configurations and operational knowledge, is consolidated into a unified reference source, improving shared understanding and reducing reliance on tacit knowledge.
6. Secure Today, Safe Tomorrow
Security is embedded at every stage of the architecture. Designing to Defra’s approved security frameworks ensures that the platform meets required standards and is resilient against current and emerging threats. The move to a cloud
‑
native security architecture enables the adoption of scalable, automated, and continuously monitored controls aligned with Cloud Centre of Excellence guidance. By retiring unsupported legacy technologies and transitioning to modern, secure services, the solution reduces exposure to vulnerabilities and establishes a sustainable security posture for the future.
7. Empower to Innovate
By removing outdated operating systems, manual IIS configurations, and brittle deployment patterns, the architecture clears long-standing barriers that have restricted innovation. The modernised platform is engineered for supportability and scalability, reducing the effort required to maintain the service and enabling teams to focus on enhancing functionality rather than fighting technical debt. Building on CCoE
‑
aligned cloud infrastructure creates a strong foundation for modern engineering practices such as DevOps, automation, and continuous improvement, unlocking opportunities for future capability expansion.
8. Right Tools, Right Place
The architecture is intentionally aligned with Defra’s approved cloud technologies, patterns, and design templates, ensuring long
‑
term technical suitability, sustainability, and governance compliance. The legacy technology stack—characterised by Windows Server 2016, IIS 10, manual scripts, and fragmented application pools—is replaced with a modern, cloud
‑
native platform tailored to the scale and complexity of the BSE service. By embedding Azure DevOps, CI/CD pipelines, and automated deployment workflows, the architecture standardises delivery across development, test, and production environments, reducing operational risk while enhancing consistency, repeatability, and engineering velocity.
Architectur
al
 
Decision
 Records
Cloud Delivery Platform
 
This decision 
favours
 Azure’s PaaS-first approach over AWS alternatives and container orchestration for DEFRA’s application modernization. Azure App Service is selected for hosting legacy .NET Framework apps due to its native support for CLR 2.0/4.0 on Windows without container overhead, offering a clean modernization path to .NET Core. Compared to AWS App Runner (Linux-only) and Amplify (front-end only), App Service delivers lower operational complexity and cost—approximately 20–30% savings versus EC2/ECS Windows. For data, Azure SQL Database and Managed Instance provide enterprise-grade features, elastic hyperscale, and simpler migrations at 25–35% lower cost than AWS RDS. Azure Entra ID ensures seamless AD integration and Windows authentication, unlike AWS IAM/Cognito. Azure Data Factory supports SSIS lift-and-shift, avoiding costly rewrites required by AWS Glue. Combined with DEFRA’s MACC discounts, this strategy minimizes TCO, accelerates modernization, and reduces operational burden through integrated, cost-efficient Azure services
ADR 1: Azure App Service vs AWS App Runner / Amplify vs Containers
Context:
DEFRA needs to host lightweight legacy .NET Framework apps and modernize them without costly containerization or operational overhead.
Options Considered:
Azure App Service
AWS App Runner / Amplify
Container orchestration (AKS/EKS)
Decision:
Use Azure App Service for hosting legacy and modern .NET apps.
Rationale:
Native Legacy .NET Framework Support: Azure App Service is purpose-built to host Windows + IIS + .NET Framework workloads natively (.NET Framework 2.0–4.8, including ASP.NET Web Forms and MVC - note: important 
version compatibility information
 and is based on CLR 2.0 and CLR 4.0 runtimes). Applications run directly on Windows with IIS without containerisation, reducing deployment complexity and governance overhead.
Modern Application Platform: Azure App Service supports a diverse selection of modern application runtimes, deployment patterns, hosting patterns, and provides a seamless upgrade path from legacy .NET Framework to modern .NET 8+, enabling customers to modernise incrementally without re-architecture. .NET 8+ delivers cross-platform support, significant performance improvements, long-term support (LTS), and enhanced security. App Service supports .NET 8+ with day-zero availability, allowing organisations to evolve applications at their own pace whilst maintaining operational simplicity. Azure App Service as a fully managed application platform enables teams utilising multiple diverse application stacks to standardise on hosting with no management overhead. App Service supports .NET, .NET Framework, NodeJS, Java, PHP, and Python. App Service also supports Windows and Linux containers for even more diverse application runtimes and both Linux and Windows hosts (Windows only for .NET Framework). Legacy applications with specialised requirements may utilise Windows Containers on App Service, with minimal additional deployment complexity, or utilise the new 
Managed Instance on App Service
 (in preview)
AWS App Runner and Amplify Limitations: AWS App Runner is a Linux-only, container-first service and does not support Windows containers. It cannot run .NET Framework applications. Only applications upgraded to .NET 8+ and containerised for Linux can be deployed to App Runner. AWS Amplify is designed for front-end JavaScript frameworks and does not support .NET workloads at all. Fallback to EC2/ECS: To run .NET Framework on AWS, customers must use Windows containers on EC2 or ECS. This introduces significant operational overhead, including infrastructure management, patching, scaling, and security hardening, none of which are required on Azure App Service.
No Containerisation Dependencies: Azure App Service runs legacy ASP.NET Framework applications as-is, with zero Docker or container knowledge required. AWS requires Windows Server deployments or Windows containerisation on ECS or EC2, adding technical complexity, infrastructure management overhead, and skill requirements.
Cost Comparison: Azure App Service Standard (S1) costs £55–£75/month (~$70–$95 USD), Premium (P1V2) costs £130–£150/month (~$165–$190 USD). AWS App Runner pricing is not applicable for .NET Framework. EC2 with Windows Server (t3.medium) costs $120–$150/month, but requires additional services (ECS, ALB, ECR), pushing total cost to $150–$200/month per workload. Azure App Service remains 20–30% more cost-effective and operationally simpler for legacy .NET workloads.
ADR 2: Azure SQL Database / Managed Instance vs AWS RDS for SQL Server
Context:
Need enterprise-grade SQL Server features, elastic scaling, and minimal downtime for migrations.
Options Considered:
Azure SQL Database / Managed Instance
AWS RDS for SQL Server
Decision:
Adopt Azure SQL Database and Managed Instance.
Rationale:
Full T-SQL and SQL Server Feature Compatibility: Azure SQL Database and Azure SQL Managed Instance (MI) are built on the same SQL Server engine and support nearly all T-SQL syntax, SQL CLR, stored procedures, and advanced features. They integrate seamlessly with .NET development tools (ADO.NET, Entity Framework, Azure DevOps) and legacy applications. AWS RDS for SQL Server offers managed SQL Server but strips critical enterprise features including PolyBase, FILESTREAM, database snapshots, SQL CLR, Resource Governor, and system-level access. Developer permissions are limited to db_owner level, restricting DBA-level operations.
Hyperscale Architecture and Elastic Scaling: Azure SQL Database offers Hyperscale architecture supporting databases up to 100TB+ with rapid scale-up/scale-down capabilities and minimal downtime. Scaling is dynamic via DTU or vCore models, with independent compute and storage scaling. AWS RDS is instance-based with vertical scaling only (up to 128 vCPU, 4TB RAM, 16TB storage max), and storage scaling requires downtime.
Easier Migration with Arc-Enabled SQL Servers: Azure now supports direct migration of Arc-enabled SQL Servers to Azure SQL Managed Instance, simplifying hybrid and on-premises to cloud transitions. This capability went GA in late 2025 and enables seamless lift-and-shift of SQL workloads with minimal disruption.
Next-Gen General Purpose Tier: Azure SQL MI introduced a Next-Gen General Purpose tier offering improved performance and greater flexibility over the standard tier. This is particularly beneficial for customers with SQL Servers hosting large numbers of databases, delivering better consolidation and cost efficiency.
Cost Comparison: Azure SQL Database pricing can start as low in the single digit Pounds range for very light workloads but typically (e.g., General Purpose, 2 vCore) costs approximately £300–£400/month (~$380–$510 USD), whilst Azure SQL Hyperscale starts at £450–£550/month (~$575–$700 USD). Azure SQL MI (Next-Gen GP, 8 vCore) is priced around £700–£850/month (~$900–$1,100 USD) depending on region and configuration. AWS RDS for SQL Server (db.m5.large, 2 vCPU, 8GB RAM, Single-AZ) costs approximately $450–$550/month including licensing. Multi-AZ deployments double this cost to $900–$1,100/month. Azure typically offers 25–35% cost savings with superior feature parity, modernisation options, and hybrid migration support.
ADR 3: Azure Entra ID vs AWS IAM and Cognito
Context:
Legacy ASP.NET apps require Windows Authentication and AD integration.
Options Considered:
Azure Entra ID
AWS IAM + Cognito
Decision:
Use Azure Entra ID for identity and access management.
Rationale:
Native Active Directory and Windows Authentication: Azure Entra ID (formerly Azure AD) is designed to integrate seamlessly with existing on-premises Active Directory, supporting Kerberos, NTLM, and Windows Integrated Authentication via Azure AD Domain Services. This is essential for legacy ASP.NET applications (Web Forms, MVC) that rely on Windows Authentication and AD-backed role resolution. AWS IAM is not an authentication provider for applications, it only controls access to AWS resources (EC2, S3, Lambda). AWS Cognito does not support Windows Authentication, Kerberos, NTLM, or AD-backed authentication and is built for consumer identity scenarios, not workforce identity.
SQL Server Authentication Integration: Azure Entra ID enables identity continuity for SQL Database workloads, providing Azure AD-based authentication to Azure SQL Database without additional configuration. AWS Cognito cannot authenticate users to SQL Server. To enable AD authentication for RDS SQL Server, AWS requires AWS Directory Service (AWS Managed Microsoft AD), which is limited in functionality and harder to integrate compared to native Azure Entra ID integration.
Cost Comparison: Azure Entra ID Free is included with Azure and Microsoft 365 subscriptions at no additional cost for basic features. Azure Entra ID P1 (required for Conditional Access and AD integration) costs $6.00/user/month (~£4.70), whilst P2 (with Identity Protection) is $9.00/user/month (~£7.00). AWS Cognito charges $0.0055 per MAU (Monthly Active User) for the first 50,000 MAUs in the Essentials tier, equating to approximately $275/month for 50,000 users. However, Cognito lacks Windows Authentication, AD integration, and SQL Server authentication, features essential for legacy .NET workloads. For workforce identity, Azure Entra ID provides comprehensive AD compatibility at a predictable per-user cost, whilst AWS requires AWS Managed Microsoft AD at $0.05/hour (~$36/month) per directory plus complexity in integration.
ADR 4: Azure Data Factory vs AWS Glue and Data Pipeline
Context:
ETL workloads rely on SSIS rewrites are costly and time-consuming.
Options Considered:
Azure Data Factory
AWS Glue / Data Pipeline
Decision:
Use Azure Data Factory for ETL and SSIS integration.
Rationale:
Native SSIS Integration:
 Azure Data Factory supports running existing SQL Server Integration Services (SSIS) packages virtually unchanged via Azure-SSIS Integration Runtime, with full compatibility for SSMS, SSDT, SSISDB, scale-out clusters, and hybrid execution. This allows lift-and-shift migration of SSIS workloads without rewrites. AWS Glue has 
no SSIS runtime support
; customers must either rewrite ETL logic in PySpark/Scala or run SSIS on self-managed EC2 instances with manual operations and no integration with AWS Glue.
Low-Code Visual Interface:
 Azure Data Factory offers drag-and-drop pipeline design, visual mapping data flows, and 
90+ built-in connectors
 (including on-premises SQL Server, SharePoint, and legacy systems). AWS Glue requires PySpark or Scala scripting with minimal low-code support; Glue Studio provides limited visual capabilities. AWS Data Pipeline's UI is outdated and lacks drag-and-drop functionality, still requiring EC2 for execution and is designed for batch data processing.
Cost Comparison:
 Azure Data Factory charges for Integration Runtime hours: 
General Purpose IR costs £0.20/hour
 (~$0.25 USD), whilst 
Azure-SSIS IR costs £0.70–£1.20/hour
 (~$0.89–$1.52 USD) depending on node size. For 100 hours/month of SSIS runtime, ADF costs approximately 
£70–£120/month
 (~$89–$152 USD). AWS Glue charges 
$0.44 per DPU-hour
 for ETL jobs. For 100 DPU-hours/month (typical for moderate ETL workloads), AWS Glue costs approximately 
$44/month
. However, AWS Glue lacks SSIS support, migrating SSIS to Glue requires complete ETL rewrites (estimated 100–300 hours of development effort at $100–$200/hour = 
$10,000–$60,000 one-off cost
). AWS Data Pipeline charges 
$1.00 per low-frequency activity
 and 
$0.60/hour for EC2-based execution
, bringing costs to 
$60–$100/month
 for similar workloads. ADF provides 
predictable, transparent pricing
 with seamless SSIS compatibility, eliminating rewrite costs and enabling 
immediate lift-and-shift migration
 with hybrid connectivity to on-premises SQL Server, .NET applications, and Azure SQL Database.
ADR 5: Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) vs AWS EKS/Fargate
Context:
While the primary strategy is PaaS-first, some workloads may require container orchestration for modernization or future scalability. The decision is between AKS and AWS EKS/Fargate.
Options Considered:
Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS)
AWS Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) with Fargate
Decision:
Use 
Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS)
 for container orchestration if required.
Rationale:
Not Recommended for Lightweight Legacy .NET Applications: For the 
BSE 
lightweight legacy .NET Framework applications, running container services introduces unnecessary overhead in terms of maintenance, operational complexity, and cost. Azure App Service (PaaS) is better suited for these workloads, providing native .NET Framework support without container orchestration.
AKS Advantages (If Containerisation is Required): If containerisation becomes necessary for modernisation or scale, AKS offers no control plane charges (free managed control plane), whilst EKS charges $0.10/hour ($72/month) per cluster for the control plane alone. AKS provides superior integration with Azure services (Entra ID, Azure Monitor, Azure DevOps), support for up to 1,000 nodes per cluster (vs. 450 per node group for EKS), up to 250 pods per node (vs. 110 for EKS), and auto-repair capabilities.
Cost Comparison: AKS control plane is free; customers pay only for worker nodes (e.g., Standard_D2s_v3 node at ~£55/month or ~$70/month). EKS charges $72/month per cluster for the control plane plus EC2 node costs (t3.medium at ~$30/month + operational overhead). For a single cluster with 3 nodes, AKS costs approximately £165–£200/month (~$210–$255 USD), whilst EKS costs $162/month (control plane + 3×t3.medium nodes) = ~$210/month minimum, with additional costs for load balancing, storage, and data transfer. For 7 lightweight applications, PaaS (App Service) remains the most cost-effective and operationally efficient choice, with estimated costs of £385–£525/month (~$490–$670 USD) for 7×Standard S1 instances vs. $1,050–$1,400/month for containerised infrastructure on either AKS or EKS.
Key Takeaways:
Azure provides a complete, integrated platform for the in-scope 
BSE 
application
 
with native Windows + IIS support, full SQL Server compatibility, and Active Directory integration, enabling organisations to run applications as-is today whilst providing a clear, low-risk path to modern .NET for long-term maintainability, performance, and security. Recent enhancements such as direct migration of Arc-enabled SQL Servers to Azure SQL Managed Instance and the Next-Gen General Purpose tier offer greater flexibility and performance - particularly for environments with many databases. Azure’s PaaS-first approach delivers 20 - 35% cost savings compared to AWS, eliminates infrastructure management overhead, and provides seamless hybrid connectivity. In contrast, AWS App Runner and Amplify do not support Windows containers or .NET Framework, requiring full re-platforming to .NET Core (.NET 8+) and containerisation. The only viable alternative for legacy .NET workloads on AWS is EC2 or ECS with Windows Server or Windows containers, which introduces significant operational complexity and cost. AWS also lacks feature parity in SQL Server services and requires workarounds or rewrites for equivalent capabilities, increasing migration risk and effort.
Architecture Framework
 
The Hub-and-Spoke architecture is chosen to securely migrate seven LAP applications built on .NET and SQL Server to Azure. This design centralizes security, monitoring, and governance while maintaining isolation for individual workloads. The hub hosts critical shared services such as Azure Firewall, Application Gateway with WAF, Microsoft Sentinel for SIEM, and Log Analytics Workspace for unified visibility. Spokes contain application VNets, ensuring least privilege and reducing blast radius. This approach aligns with Azure Landing Zone best practices, supports hybrid connectivity, and scales easily for future workloads. It delivers strong security posture, operational efficiency, and cost optimization for DEFRA’s modernization strategy.
ADR : Hub-and-Spoke Architecture for 
Migration of 
BSE Application
Context:
DEFRA is migrating 
the BSE 
application
 
built on .NET and SQL Server to Azure. The design must ensure secure connectivity, centralized security monitoring, and cost-effective scalability while supporting application-level protection
.
Options Considered:
Flat VNet design with shared resources
Hub-and-Spoke architecture with centralized security and monitoring
Multiple isolated VNets per application
Decision:
Adopt 
Hub-and-Spoke architecture
 with centralized security services in the hub.
Rationale:
Centralized Security: The hub hosts Azure Firewall and Application Gateway with WAF, providing a single point for traffic inspection and protection against OWASP Top 10 vulnerabilities. This reduces complexity compared to deploying WAF per spoke.
Monitoring &amp; Compliance: Microsoft Sentinel in the hub offers advanced SIEM capabilities, threat detection, and compliance reporting across all spokes. Log Analytics Workspace aggregates logs from applications, databases, and network resources for unified visibility.
Isolation &amp; Governance: Spokes isolate each application workload, enforcing least privilege and minimizing blast radius in case of compromise. Hub-and-Spoke aligns with Azure Landing Zone best practices for enterprise governance.
Scalability &amp; Hybrid Connectivity: The hub simplifies connectivity to on-premises networks via VPN or ExpressRoute and supports future spokes without redesign.
Cost Efficiency: Centralizing security and monitoring avoids duplication of services across spokes, reducing operational overhead and licensing costs.
Key Takeaways 
Implementing Hub-and-Spoke ensures centralized security and monitoring, reducing complexity and cost compared to duplicating services across VNets. Application Gateway with WAF in the hub protects against common web threats, while Microsoft Sentinel and Log Analytics provide unified threat detection and compliance reporting. Spoke isolation enforces least privilege and minimizes risk exposure. The design supports hybrid connectivity and future scalability without major redesign. While initial setup is more complex, the long-term benefits include simplified governance, strong security posture, and operational efficiency. This architecture is a strategic fit for DEFRA’s modernization, aligning with enterprise best practices and cost optimization goals.

Risks
Ref
Description
Impact
Mitigation
R
001
Unclear runtime baseline (ASP.NET 2.0 vs 4.0)
 – Documentation references ASP.NET Web Forms on .NET Framework 4.0, while other sections still imply CLR 2.0. An incorrect baseline invalidates remediation, upgrade, testing, and CVE assumptions.
High
 – Incorrect baseline leads to failed upgrade, rework, and potential go
live delays.
Confirm runtime by inspecting IIS application pool, CLR version, web.config, referenced assemblies, and build artifacts. Document and approve a single authoritative baseline before remediation.
R
002
.NET runtime uplift risk (4.0 → 4.8.x)
 – Upgrading to a supported .NET version may introduce breaking changes (deprecated APIs, binding redirects, third
party DLL incompatibility).
High
 – Application instability or functional regression post
migration.
Early compatibility testing in non
prod, dependency audit, regression test execution, and App Service deployment slots with rollback support.
R
003
Identity cutover risk (Windows Authentication → Entra ID)
 – Migration to Entra ID may break authentication or authorization due to incorrect claims mapping, group resolution, or role enforcement.
High
 – User lockout or unintended access escalation.
Parallel authentication testing, agreed role
to
group mapping, claims validation, break
glass Entra admin accounts, and phased cutover.
R
004
Private Endpoint / Private DNS misconfiguration
 – Incorrect DNS zone linkage, forwarding, or hub resolver configuration may break connectivity between App Service, Azure SQL, ADF, or Key Vault.
High
 – Application outage or loss of data connectivity.
Adopt CCoE
approved DNS pattern, validate connectivity in non
prod, perform end
to
end private endpoint testing, manage DNS via IaC.
R
005
ADF connectivity failure to TSE systems
 – Data ingestion pipelines depend on correct routing, firewall rules, and private endpoints; misconfiguration could halt data synchronisation.
High
 – Loss of surveillance data and reporting inaccuracies.
Test connectivity in non
prod first, restrict access via least
privilege network rules, enable retries/alerts, document rerun procedures.
R
006
Data migration and cutover inconsistency
 – Differences between on
prem SQL Server and Azure SQL (collation, compatibility level, unsupported features) may cause data issues post
cutover.
High
 – Data integrity issues or rollback requirement.
Use Azure Migrate and DMS assessment, schema and row
count validation, business data reconciliation, parallel run and rollback plan.
R
007
Direct database access governance risk (AVD/SSMS)
 – Misconfiguration could allow excessive privileges, cross
database access, or uncontrolled data extraction despite read
only intent.
High
 – Data governance and compliance breach.
Enforce Entra
only authentication, db_datareader roles, deny write permissions, firewall allow
listing from AVD only, PIM/JIT, SQL auditing and Sentinel alerts.
R
008
Residual CVE exposure during remediation window
 – Legacy libraries, NuGet dependencies, or TLS settings may remain vulnerable until full uplift is completed.
High
 – Security exposure and audit findings.
Enforce SAST and dependency scanning in CI/CD, Defender for App Service and SQL, TLS 1.2+, WAF rules, rapid patch cycle, documented risk acceptance if required.
R
009
Incomplete handover from Civica
 – Missing source code, SSIS packages, certificates, or environment documentation may delay migration and testing.
High
 – Delivery delays and reliance on vendor.
Formal handover checklist, early validation builds, acceptance criteria sign
off before UAT and production cutover.
R
010
Operational readiness gap post
cutover
 – Support teams may lack runbooks or experience with Azure PaaS operations, impacting incident response.
Medium
 – Increased MTTR and instability after go
live.
Produce runbooks (identity, DNS, ADF, SQL, App Service), monitored cutover, warranty support period, and operational handover.

A-002
No Functional Change
 - Only infrastructure ownership will change — not UI or functional behaviour.
If functional changes occur, additional testing, user training, and change management will be required, increasing timelines and risk of defects.
A-00
3
Defra Security Policies Will Be Applied
 - Identity, access management, and auditing will align with Defra policies
If security policies are not enforced, there will be compliance breaches, audit failures, and increased risk of unauthorized access.
A-00
4
Upgrading .NET version
 - As part of the cloud migration and re
‑
hosting activity, the application may need to be upgraded from its existing .NET 2.0 runtime to a higher, supported .NET version to ensure compatibility, security, and maintainability in the new environment.
If .NET upgrade is not feasible or delayed, application may not run in the new environment, causing migration failure and extended downtime.
A-00
5
Azure Environment Availability - Defra’s Azure environment and governance framework are established and available for the project.
 
 
If Azure environment or governance is not ready, hosting and deployment will be blocked, delaying migration and increasing costs.
A-00

CCoE Compliance
 
- 
All infrastructure and integrations comply with CCoE standards, tagging conventions and security baselines.
 
 
If infrastructure does not meet CCoE standards, it will fail compliance checks, require rework and delay go live.
